Reward Score Matching: Unifying Reward-based Fine-tuning for Flow and Diffusion Models

Jeongjae Lee*    Jinho Chang*    Jeongsol Kim†    Jong Chul Ye† Affiliation: Graduate School of AI Affiliation: KAIST, Korea Affiliation: {jaylee2000, jinhojsk515, jeongsol, jong.ye}@kaist.ac.kr Affiliation: *First authors    †Corresponding authors
Abstract

Reward-based fine-tuning aims to steer a pretrained diffusion or flow-based generative model toward higher-reward samples while remaining close to the pretrained model. Although existing methods are motivated by different perspectives such as Soft RL, GFlowNets, etc., we show that many can be written under a common framework, which we call reward score matching (RSM). Under this view, alignment becomes score matching toward a reward-guided target, and the main differences across methods reduce to the construction of the value-guidance estimator and the effective optimization strength across timesteps. This unification clarifies the bias–variance–compute tradeoffs of existing designs and distinguishes core optimization components from auxiliary mechanisms that add complexity without clear benefit. Guided by this perspective, we develop simpler redesigns that improve alignment effectiveness and compute efficiency across representative settings with differentiable and black-box rewards. Overall, RSM turns a seemingly fragmented collection of reward-based fine-tuning methods into a smaller, more interpretable, and more actionable design space.

1 Introduction

Reward-based fine-tuning seeks to steer a pretrained diffusion or flow-based generative model toward higher-reward samples without deviating too far from the pretrained model. This problem has recently attracted a wide range of methods, including entropy-regularized reinforcement learning (Soft RL) [3, 9, 50, 24, 20, 12, 21], optimal control [26], and GFlowNets [51, 27, 25]. As a result, the literature appears fragmented: methods are presented with different objectives, derivations, and stabilization heuristics, making it difficult to tell which differences are fundamental and which are merely implementational.

In this paper, we show that many such methods reduce to a single underlying objective, which we term Reward Score Matching (RSM; see Table 1). At a high level, reward alignment can be viewed as score matching toward an ideal reward-guided target distribution which is composed of a reference term and an effective value-guidance term, together with timestep-dependent weighting or trust-region control. This unified view also clarifies the key distinction across methods.

In practice, this target is intractable to compute in high dimensions, so existing methods replace it with tractable value-guidance surrogates. Accordingly, the primary difference lies in how the value-guidance surrogate is constructed: some methods directly compute reward gradients, while others rely solely on reward evaluations, estimating the same signal through sampling. Applying Stein’s identity [38], one of the most important contributions of this work is to show that these two strategies correspond precisely to first-order and zeroth-order estimations of a common underlying target, respectively.

This reduction is especially revealing for policy-gradient methods: using PCPO’s clipped log-ratio surrogate [20], we show that the PPO-clip objective also admits the same score-matching L2L_{2} form. Furthermore, methods derived from seemingly different viewpoints such as GFlowNet and direct regression objectives often do not optimize fundamentally different targets, but rather different tractable surrogates of the same reward-guided score-matching problem.

Once this distinction is isolated, the remaining design space can be studied on common ground: estimator design determines guidance quality, temporal weighting scales its magnitude across timesteps, and trust-region realization determines how much of it survives regularization. This decomposition also helps separate core optimization ingredients from auxiliary mechanisms that add theoretical structure or implementation complexity without clearly improving the underlying update.

A second contribution of this paper is to use this unified framework as a practical diagnostic tool. RSM reveals shared bias–variance–compute tradeoffs across methods that would otherwise appear unrelated. For example, first-order Tweedie-based guidance can be simple but biased, especially at low-SNR timesteps, whereas zeroth-order full-rollout guidance can be unbiased but noisy and compute-intensive. Likewise, several recently proposed components can be reinterpreted as secondary coefficient-level modifications rather than distinct algorithmic principles. This yields a more systematic lens on the design space and explains why some inherited choices are more consequential than others.

Guided by this perspective, we show that several seemingly important design choices are secondary, while a few principled changes drive most of the practical improvements. Specifically, by comparing their value-guidance estimators through shared bias–variance–compute tradeoffs, we show that some auxiliary components can be removed without hurting performance. These insights lead to simple redesigns that improve alignment quality while reducing compute cost across representative differentiable-reward and black-box-reward settings, including a 5×5\times wall-clock speedup over TempFlow-GRPO [12] on the GenEval reward [11].

2.3 Training-based Reward Alignment

Soft RL formulates alignment as an entropy-regularized Markov decision process over discretized reverse-time transitions [2, 3, 9, 41]. With timesteps 0=t0<t1<⋯<tN=10=t_{0}<t_{1}<\dots<t_{N}=1, the state is 𝒙t∈ℝd{\bm{x}}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, the learnable reverse transition pθ​(𝒙ti−1∣𝒙ti)p^{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}}\mid{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}) is the time-indexed policy, and reward is received only at the terminal state. This yields the objective

maxθ𝔼𝒙0∼p0θ[r(𝒙0)]−α∑i𝒟KL(pθ(⋅|𝒙ti)∥pref(⋅|𝒙ti)).\max_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{x}}_{0}\sim p_{0}^{\theta}}[r({\bm{x}}_{0})]-\alpha\sum_{i}\mathcal{D}_{\text{KL}}(p^{\theta}(\cdot|{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}})\|p^{\text{ref}}(\cdot|{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}})). (9)

A key object is the soft value function Vt​(𝒙t)V_{t}({\bm{x}}_{t}), which combines future reward and entropy regularization. The corresponding optimal marginal satisfies

pt⋆​(𝒙t)=ptref​(𝒙t)Z​exp⁡(Vt​(𝒙t)α),p_{t}^{\star}({\bm{x}}_{t})=\frac{p_{t}^{\text{ref}}({\bm{x}}_{t})}{Z}\exp\Big(\frac{V_{t}({\bm{x}}_{t})}{\alpha}\Big), (10)

where ZZ is a normalizing constant independent of tt [41]. Soft RL subsumes Residual ∇\nabla-DB [27], SQDF [18], and policy-gradient methods.

Several alignment methods are not fully captured by Soft RL. VGG-Flow [26] and DiffusionNFT [52] directly regress the model velocity field toward a reward-guided target. Several recent methods also introduce timestep-dependent weighting [12, 20, 45, 4] to improve stability and convergence, mirroring the use of reweighting in diffusion pretraining [13]. In the next section, we show that many of these methods can be unified under a common RSM formulation33 3 DiffusionNFT remains closely related but does not reduce exactly to the same formulation; see Appendix H.3., which also provides a systematic lens on temporal weighting.

3 Reward Score Matching: A Unified Framework

This decomposition highlights three competing forces: Effective Guidance steers generation toward high rewards, while KL Regularization and the Trust Region term prevent model collapse by anchoring the model to the reference and previous policies, respectively. Section 3.1 is written in the entropy-regularized setting for generality, but Eq. (15) also reconciles the α=0\alpha=0 case for SQDF [18] and policy-gradient methods; see Appendix C for details.

Eq. (15) also clarifies the hierarchy of RSM’s design dimensions. The primary source of variation between methods lies in the way 𝚿^ti{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}\hat{\mathbf{\Psi}}_{t_{i}}} is constructed. By contrast, temporal weighting and trust-region realization act only as secondary coefficient-level modifiers via γ⁡(ti),C1​(ti),C2​(ti)\gamma(t_{i}),C_{1}(t_{i}),C_{2}(t_{i}) and clipping. We therefore focus first on estimator design, and defer these coefficient-level choices to Section 4.

3.2 Estimating Optimal Value Guidance 𝚿^ti{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}\hat{\mathbf{\Psi}}_{t_{i}}}

This section, which is one of the most important contributions of this paper, shows that the seemingly different forms of reward-based finetuning methods can be unified as the zeroth and first order estimate of the current or lookahead estimator of the optimal value guidance estimate. Specifically, Eq. (12) suggests two practical families of value-guidance estimators: current-state and lookahead.

Current-state Estimator. Recall the first equality in Eq. (12):

𝚿ti⋆=1α​∇𝒙tiVti​(𝒙ti)\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\mathbf{\Psi}^{\star}_{t_{i}}}=\frac{1}{\alpha}\nabla_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}}V_{t_{i}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}) (16)

This suggests a current-state estimator, available only in the first-order setting. VGG-Flow [26] falls in this family. Specifically, since we do not have access to the value function VV but only to the terminal reward rr, we approximate 𝚿ti⋆{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\mathbf{\Psi}_{t_{i}}^{\star}} directly at 𝒙ti{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}} via a Tweedie estimate.

Definition 3.4 (Current-state Estimator).

The first-order current-state estimator is

𝚿^tiCS,1\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}\hat{\mathbf{\Psi}}_{t_{i}}^{\mathrm{CS},1}} =1α​∇𝒙tir​(𝒙^0|ti)≈1α​∇𝒙tiVti​(𝒙ti).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\alpha}\nabla_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}}r(\hat{\bm{x}}_{0|t_{i}})\;\approx\;\frac{1}{\alpha}\nabla_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}}V_{t_{i}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}). (17)

This avoids the stochastic rollout but incurs substantial bias at low-SNR timesteps, as will be discussed later. It is therefore best viewed as a simpler but more biased alternative to lookahead estimators explained below, which subsumes most existing methods and exposes the main design tradeoffs.

Lookahead Estimator. Lookahead estimators roll out from 𝒙ti{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}} to 𝒙tj{\bm{x}}_{t_{j}} with j<ij<i and extract reward information there. First-order estimators require differentiable rewards, whereas zeroth-order estimators apply to arbitrary black-box rewards.

Definition 3.5 (Lookahead Estimators).

For lookahead depth j<ij<i and branching width KiK_{i}, the first-order and zeroth-order lookahead estimators are

𝚿^tiLA,1\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}\hat{\mathbf{\Psi}}_{t_{i}}^{\mathrm{LA},1}} =σti2α​Ω​(ti)​1Ki​∑k=1Ki∇𝒙ti−1(k)r​(𝒙^0|tj(k))\displaystyle=\frac{\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}}{\alpha\Omega(t_{i})}\frac{1}{K_{i}}\sum_{k=1}^{K_{i}}\nabla_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}}^{(k)}}r(\hat{\bm{x}}_{0|t_{j}}^{(k)}) ≈\displaystyle\;\approx\; σti2α​Ω​(ti)𝔼𝒙ti−1:tj[∇𝒙ti−1r(𝒙^0|tj)],\displaystyle\frac{\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}}{\alpha\Omega(t_{i})}\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}:t_{j}}}\Big[\nabla_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}}}r(\hat{\bm{x}}_{0|t_{j}})\Big], (18)
𝚿^tiLA,0\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}\hat{\mathbf{\Psi}}_{t_{i}}^{\mathrm{LA},0}} =σtiα​Ω​(ti)​1Ki​∑k=1Kir⁡(𝒙^0|tj(k))​ϵti(k)\displaystyle=\frac{\sigma_{t_{i}}}{\alpha\Omega(t_{i})}\frac{1}{K_{i}}\sum_{k=1}^{K_{i}}r(\hat{\bm{x}}_{0|t_{j}}^{(k)})\,{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}}^{(k)} ≈\displaystyle\;\approx\; σtiα​Ω​(ti)𝔼𝒙ti−1:tj[r(𝒙^0|tj)ϵti],\displaystyle\frac{\sigma_{t_{i}}}{\alpha\Omega(t_{i})}\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}:t_{j}}}\Big[r(\hat{\bm{x}}_{0|t_{j}})\,{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}}\Big], (19)

where 𝒙^0|tj\hat{\bm{x}}_{0|t_{j}} denotes the Tweedie estimate of the posterior mean:

𝒙^0|tj=𝔼⁡[𝒙0∣𝒙tj]:=𝔼𝒙0∼ptj​(𝒙0∣𝒙tj)​[𝒙0].\displaystyle\hat{\bm{x}}_{0|t_{j}}=\mathbb{E}[{\bm{x}}_{0}\mid{\bm{x}}_{t_{j}}]:=\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{x}}_{0}\sim p_{t_{j}}({\bm{x}}_{0}\mid{\bm{x}}_{t_{j}})}\!\left[{\bm{x}}_{0}\right]. (20)

Existing first-order lookahead methods (Residual ∇\nabla-DB [27], SQDF [18]) use one-step lookahead (j=i−1j=i-1), and therefore inherit substantial Tweedie bias from 𝒙^0|tj\hat{{\bm{x}}}_{0|t_{j}} at low-SNR timesteps, akin to current-state methods (j=ij=i).

Several first-order methods (Residual ∇\nabla-DB, VGG-Flow) attempt to decompose the soft value gradient into a Tweedie approximation, and learn the residual Jensen gap via a small neural network gϕg_{\phi}, which can be explained by Proposition 3.6. See Appendix B.3 for the proof.

Proposition 3.6 (Conditional Consistency of First-Order Estimators).

Let j∈{i,i−1}j\in\{i,\,i-1\}. Suppose that the soft value gradient at timestep tjt_{j} admits the exact decomposition

∇𝒙tjVtj​(𝒙tj)=γti​∇𝒙tjr​(𝒙^0|tj)+gϕ​(𝒙tj).\nabla_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{j}}}V_{t_{j}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{j}})=\gamma_{t_{i}}\nabla_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{j}}}r(\hat{\bm{x}}_{0\mid t_{j}})+g_{\phi}({\bm{x}}_{t_{j}}). (21)

Define the residual-corrected first-order estimator

𝚿^tiFO,res(j):=(1αι[j=i]+σti2α​Ω​(ti)ι[j=i−1])(γti∇𝒙tjr(𝒙^0|tj)+gϕ(𝒙tj)),{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}\hat{\mathbf{\Psi}}_{t_{i}}^{\mathrm{FO,res}}(j)}:=\left(\frac{1}{\alpha}\iota[j=i]+\frac{\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}}{\alpha\Omega(t_{i})}\iota[j=i-1]\right)\Big(\gamma_{t_{i}}\nabla_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{j}}}r(\hat{\bm{x}}_{0\mid t_{j}})+g_{\phi}({\bm{x}}_{t_{j}})\Big), (22)

where ι⁡[⋅]\iota[\,\cdot\,] denotes the indicator function, and for j=i−1j=i-1 we take 𝐱ti−1∼pti⋆(⋅∣𝐱ti){\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}}\sim p^{\star}_{t_{i}}(\cdot\mid{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}), while for j=ij=i we simply set 𝐱tj=𝐱ti{\bm{x}}_{t_{j}}={\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}. Then

𝔼⁡[𝚿^tiFO,res​(j)|𝒙ti]=𝚿ti⋆​(𝒙ti),\mathbb{E}\!\left[{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}\hat{\mathbf{\Psi}}_{t_{i}}^{\mathrm{FO,res}}(j)}\;\middle|\;{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}\right]={\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\mathbf{\Psi}_{t_{i}}^{\star}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}), (23)

where the expectation is trivial in the current-state case j=ij=i. That is, under an exact residual parameterization gϕg_{\phi}, both the current-state first-order estimator and the one-step first-order estimator are unbiased for the optimal value guidance.

Under an exact residual parameterization, the resulting estimator is unbiased. However, as we later verify in Appendix G.1, auxiliary corrections gϕg_{\phi} turns out to be effectively negligible in the existing methods, so the resulting first-order estimators remain biased.

Existing zeroth-order (policy-gradient) methods typically use full rollout (j=0j=0)66 6 In principle, first-order consistency can also be achieved by full rollout, i.e. by selecting j=0j=0 and differentiating the terminal reward through the entire denoising trajectory. However, this requires the full Jacobian chain and is therefore computationally impractical and potentially unstable in high dimension. . This full-rollout zeroth-order estimator is unbiased for the soft value gradient. Notably, the following theorem, originated from Stein’s identity [38], completes the theoretical unification of zeroth-order and first-order value-guidance methods. The proof can be found in Appendix B.4.

Theorem 3.7 (Consistency of Policy Gradient).

For the full-rollout j=0j=0, the lookahead zeroth-order estimator is an unbiased estimator of the soft value gradient:

𝚿^tiLA,0\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}\hat{\mathbf{\Psi}}_{t_{i}}^{\mathrm{LA},0}} ≈σtiα​Ω​(ti)𝔼ϵti:t0∼iid𝒩(𝟎,𝐈)[r(𝒙0)ϵti]=𝔼ϵti[σti2α​Ω​(ti)∇𝒙ti−1Vti−1(𝒙ti−1)]=𝚿⋆ti.\displaystyle\approx\frac{\sigma_{t_{i}}}{\alpha\Omega(t_{i})}\mathbb{E}_{{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}:t_{0}}\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})}[r({\bm{x}}_{0}){\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}}]=\mathbb{E}_{{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}}}[\frac{\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}}{\alpha\Omega(t_{i})}\nabla_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}}}V_{t_{i-1}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}})]={\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\mathbf{\Psi}^{\star}_{t_{i}}}. (24)

Approximating the lookahead expectation with sampled descendants introduces two further design choices to reduce variance. Branching specifies per-step branch widths KiK_{i}, with Ki=1K_{i}=1 denoting a point estimate at tit_{i}; larger KiK_{i} reduce variance at higher compute cost [22, 12]. Stochasticity localization changes the underlying stochastic control problem by keeping only selected reverse steps stochastic [21, 12]. This reduces the accumulation of variance, giving a more cost-effective estimate of 𝚿ti⋆{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\mathbf{\Psi}_{t_{i}}^{\star}}.

4 Practical Design Choices of RSM from Optimization Perspectives

Section 3 established exact reductions: many existing methods can be written under a common RSM objective. We now shift from this probabilistic view to a practical optimization view, asking which design choices matter most under finite compute and noisy gradient estimates. From this perspective, performance is governed by three coupled design dimensions: estimator design, temporal weighting, and trust-region realization. Estimator design controls the quality of the value-guidance estimate, while temporal weighting and trust-region realization determine how strongly each timestep is optimized and regularized. Existing methods therefore differ mainly in how they allocate compute, optimization mass, and regularization across timesteps.

Estimator design determines the quality of 𝚿^ti{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}\hat{\mathbf{\Psi}}_{t_{i}}}. Its main practical knobs are lookahead depth jj, branching width {Ki}\{K_{i}\}, and stochasticity localization. Deeper lookahead reduces bias at higher compute cost, while larger branching widths reduce finite-sample variance at higher cost. Stochasticity localization can likewise improve estimator quality, but unlike branching, it also changes the underlying stochastic control problem. Under fixed compute, estimator design therefore asks how much budget to spend on deeper rollouts, more descendants, and where to place stochastic steps. This induces two allocation problems: how to divide compute within each timestep to obtain a useful guidance estimate, and how to distribute total estimator budget across timesteps.

An important example is the zeroth-order estimator, whose exact conditional variance under independent descendant rollouts is 1Ki​(σtiα​Ω​(ti))2​Cov​(r⁡(𝒙0)​ϵti∣𝒙ti)\frac{1}{K_{i}}\left(\frac{\sigma_{t_{i}}}{\alpha\Omega(t_{i})}\right)^{2}\mathrm{Cov}\!\left(r({\bm{x}}_{0}){\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}}\mid{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}\right). Accordingly, conditioned on 𝒙ti{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}, the covariance of the full-rollout zeroth-order estimator 𝚿^tiLA,0{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}\hat{\mathbf{\Psi}}_{t_{i}}^{\text{LA},0}} scales as:

Cov⁡(𝚿^tiLA,0∣𝒙ti)∝∼1Ki​(σtiα​Ω​(ti))2.\mathrm{Cov}\!\left({\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}\hat{\mathbf{\Psi}}_{t_{i}}^{\text{LA},0}}\mid{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}\right)\mathrel{\vbox{\halign{\hfil$#$\hfil\cr\propto\cr\kern 1.0pt\cr\sim\cr}}}\frac{1}{K_{i}}\left(\frac{\sigma_{t_{i}}}{\alpha\Omega(t_{i})}\right)^{2}. (25)

Note that this scaling should be read as leading-order scaling. This scaling shows that, under a fixed branching width Ki{K_{i}}, some timesteps are intrinsically noisier than others and may therefore require larger KiK_{i} to reduce variance, at the cost of additional compute.

Estimator design also includes reward centering; for instance, subtracting the sample mean acts as a control variate that reduces estimator variance without changing the underlying target guidance.

Temporal weighting. From an optimization perspective, the key question is not only how 𝚿^ti{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}\hat{\mathbf{\Psi}}_{t_{i}}} is estimated, but how strongly its reward signal enters the actual update at each timestep. Recall from the Canonical Gradient Form in Eq. (15) that the effective guidance term appears through 𝚿ti{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathbf{\Psi}_{t_{i}}}, and that practical methods define 𝚿ti​(𝒙ti):=γ⁡(ti)​𝚿^ti​(𝒙ti){\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathbf{\Psi}_{t_{i}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i}})}:=\gamma(t_{i}){\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}\hat{\mathbf{\Psi}}_{t_{i}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i}})}. We therefore seek a common coefficient that measures the timestep-wise optimization strength of the underlying reward signal.

For current-state estimators, Eq. (17) shows that 𝚿^ti{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}\hat{\mathbf{\Psi}}_{t_{i}}} is proportional to a reward gradient at the current state. For lookahead estimators, combining Theorem 3.7 with Eqs. (18)–(19) yields the common reward-gradient view

∇r​(𝒙ti)^=1σti𝔼𝒙ti:t0[r(𝒙0)ϵti]=𝔼𝒙ti:t0[∇𝒙ti−1r(𝒙0)].\widehat{\nabla r({\bm{x}}_{t_{i}})}=\frac{1}{\sigma_{t_{i}}}\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}:t_{0}}}\big[r({\bm{x}}_{0}){\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}}\big]=\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}:t_{0}}}\big[\nabla_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}}}r({\bm{x}}_{0})\big]. (26)

Thus, both differentiable-reward and black-box-reward methods can be compared through a common reward-gradient signal. Accordingly, the canonical gradient form in Eq. (14) can be represented with respect to the common reward-gradient Eq. (26).

More specifically, by using additional conversion factor δ⁡(t)\delta(t) between score guidance and actual optimization dynamics (see Appendix D.2) such that −δ⁡(t)​(ϵtθ−ϵtref)=𝒔tθ-\delta(t)({\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}^{\theta}_{t}-{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}^{\text{ref}}_{t})={\bm{s}}^{\theta}_{t} for ϵ{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}-prediction or −δ⁡(t)​(𝒗tθ−𝒗tref)=𝒔tθ-\delta(t)({\bm{v}}^{\theta}_{t}-{\bm{v}}^{\text{ref}}_{t})={\bm{s}}^{\theta}_{t} for 𝒗{\bm{v}}-prediction, respectively, the canonical gradient can be represented by

∇θℒ​(θ)=2​𝔼​[𝐉θ​(𝒈tiθ)⊤​𝒢~​(𝒙ti)],\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}(\theta)=2\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{J}_{\theta}({\bm{g}}_{t_{i}}^{\theta})^{\top}\tilde{\mathcal{G}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i}})], (27)

where

𝒢~​(𝒙ti)=h⁡(ti)​∇r​(𝒙ti)^+δ​(ti)2​C1​(ti)​((𝒈tiθ−𝒈tiref)⏟KL Regularization+C2​(ti)​(𝒈tiθ−𝒈tiθ†)⏟Trust Region).\tilde{\mathcal{G}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i}})=h(t_{i})\widehat{\nabla r({\bm{x}}_{t_{i}})}+\delta(t_{i})^{2}C_{1}(t_{i})\bigg(\underbrace{\big({\bm{g}}^{\theta}_{t_{i}}-{\bm{g}}^{\text{ref}}_{t_{i}}\big)}_{\text{KL Regularization}}+C_{2}(t_{i})\underbrace{\big({\bm{g}}^{\theta}_{t_{i}}-{\bm{g}}^{\theta^{\dagger}}_{t_{i}}\big)}_{\text{Trust Region}}\bigg). (28)

where 𝒈θ{\bm{g}}^{\theta} denotes the neural network parameterization (e.g., 𝒈θ=ϵθ{\bm{g}}^{\theta}={\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}^{\theta} for ϵ{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}-prediction or 𝒈θ=𝒗θ{\bm{g}}^{\theta}={\bm{v}}^{\theta} for 𝒗{\bm{v}}-prediction, respectively), and h⁡(ti)h(t_{i}) refers to the combined timestep-wise coefficient of the reward-gradient signal in the update as the Normalized Influence Metric:

h⁡(ti):=δ⁡(ti)​C1​(ti)×{γ⁡(ti)/α,(current-state),γ⁡(ti)​σti2/(α​Ω​(ti)),(lookahead).h(t_{i}):=\delta(t_{i})C_{1}(t_{i})\times\begin{cases}\gamma(t_{i})/\alpha,&(\text{current-state}),\\ \gamma(t_{i})\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}/(\alpha\Omega(t_{i})),&(\text{lookahead}).\end{cases} (29)

In other words, h⁡(t)h(t) measures how strongly the reward gradient enters optimization dynamics after accounting for both temporal weighting and parameterization. Plots for representative methods are shown in Fig. 1.

This view reveals a clear empirical contrast. Successful first-order methods place most of the mass of h⁡(t)h(t) on high-SNR timesteps, suppressing low-SNR timesteps where its estimators are most biased. For zeroth-order methods, the situation is reversed: the estimator is unbiased, but high-SNR timesteps have higher variance under fixed branching width (Eq. (25)). Thus, improved methods place more mass of h⁡(t)h(t) on low-SNR timesteps.

Temporal weighting also includes any normalization that rescales rewards or advantages. Unlike centering, which acts as a control variate, dividing by a sample-dependent scale changes the effective guidance magnitude and therefore belongs conceptually with temporal weighting.

Trust-region realization determines how much of the update signal survives. In our formulation, it appears through C2​(t)C_{2}(t) and clipping. Even with the same estimator quality and temporal weighting, different trust-region realizations can produce very different effective updates across timesteps. Timestep emphasis therefore depends not only on how strongly a timestep is weighted, but also on how much of its proposed update survives regularization and clipping. See Table 1 for the existing choices of this parameter.

5 Experiments

Inspired by our theoretical findings, we study the practical design space of RSM in two stages. First, we isolate estimator design at a single timestep under fixed compute, asking which local allocations estimate 𝚿ti⋆{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\mathbf{\Psi}_{t_{i}}^{\star}} most effectively. Second, we study end-to-end design under fixed total compute, asking how estimator design, temporal weighting, and trust-region realization should be chosen jointly across timesteps.

5.1 Isolated Estimator Analysis

Setup. We construct a two-dimensional toy problem with analytically tractable 𝚿ti⋆{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\mathbf{\Psi}_{t_{i}}^{\star}}, where a Gaussian-mixture reference distribution p0ref​(𝒙0)p_{0}^{\mathrm{ref}}({\bm{x}}_{0}) is reward-tilted into p0⋆​(𝒙0)p_{0}^{\star}({\bm{x}}_{0}). We then compare estimators 𝚿^tiLA{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}\hat{\mathbf{\Psi}}_{t_{i}}^{\text{LA}}} from Eqs. (18)–(19) against this ground truth by RMSE under matched compute. See Appendix E.1 for details.

Results. Fig. 8(b) shows that one-step lookahead first-order guidance is severely biased at low SNR. By contrast, full-rollout zeroth-order guidance is unbiased, but requires many more samples for reliable estimates. Reward centering further reduces zeroth-order error at fixed sample count.

Fig. 8(c-i) shows that lookahead depth jj induces a three-way tradeoff among bias, variance, and compute. Deeper lookahead reduces bias, but under limited samples shallower lookahead can be both more accurate and more compute-efficient, since it averages over posterior uncertainty and therefore has lower variance than full rollout; this is especially clear in the zeroth-order results. At the same lookahead depth, the first-order estimator typically improves faster with sample count than the zeroth-order estimator99 9 In this toy analysis, first-order curves use the full Jacobian chain to compute the exact first-order signal..

Fig. 8(c-ii) shows that, under fixed total sample budget, different branching patterns yield similar error--NFE trends1010 10 Note that branching improves the conditional estimate for a given parent latent, but under fixed sample budget it reduces the number of distinct parent latents explored at that timestep. This tradeoff is not fully captured by our toy analysis, but is important in practice.. Fig. 8(c-iii) shows that stochasticity localization improves estimator quality by making the induced value function easier to predict under fixed compute 1111 11 As discussed in Section 3.2, this benefit comes partly from changing the underlying stochastic control problem rather than merely reducing variance for the same target..

Findings. Under finite compute, the best local estimator need not be the least biased one: shallower lookahead estimators may outperform unbiased full-rollout estimators when variance and cost dominate. Our results also suggest that point estimates are too noisy, but once branching is used at all, the specific (#​split,#​branch)(\#\text{split},\#\text{branch}) choice matters relatively little under matched sample budget. We also find that subtracting the sample mean is crucial to reduce estimate variance.

5.2 End-to-End Design

We now test whether aforementioned design principles improve end-to-end optimization under matched compute. Experiment details are in Appendix E; note that our proposed improvements require comparable or significantly less compute per epoch compared to baselines. More results are in Appendices F.1 and I.

Mechanistic Analysis. We begin with a diagnostic case study on zeroth-order flow matching, using TempFlow-GRPO as the baseline. By Eq (25), we can conjecture that zeroth-order guidance at high-SNR timesteps is intrinsically noisy under fixed branching width. TempFlow-GRPO nevertheless assigns substantial budget to these timesteps, while relying on strong clipping and downweighting to contain the resulting instability. This suggests a mismatch between where compute is spent and where guidance is actually reliable.

We therefore redesign the update in three steps. First, we make clipping comparable across timesteps by moving the timestep-dependent scale outside the clipping operator:

clipξ​(‖μtiθ−μtiθ†‖22​σ~ti2​Δ​ti)⟶1σ~ti2​Δ​ti​clipξ​(‖μtiθ−μtiθ†‖22).\text{clip}_{\xi}\!\left(\frac{\|\mu_{t_{i}}^{\theta}-\mu_{t_{i}}^{\theta^{\dagger}}\|^{2}}{2\tilde{\sigma}_{t_{i}}^{2}\Delta t_{i}}\right)\;\longrightarrow\;\frac{1}{\tilde{\sigma}_{t_{i}}^{2}\Delta t_{i}}\text{clip}_{\xi}\!\left(\frac{\|\mu_{t_{i}}^{\theta}-\mu_{t_{i}}^{\theta^{\dagger}}\|^{2}}{2}\right). (30)

Second, we reallocate branching budget toward the high-SNR region to reduce estimator variance where it is largest. Third, once this redistribution is applied, we find that t9t_{9} remains too noisy and too heavily clipped to justify further investment, so we deactivate it and reallocate its budget to the remaining steps.

Fig. 3 shows that uniform redistribution already improves over TempFlow-GRPO, and a variance-aware redistribution performs best. Under matched compute, this redesign improves reward more quickly while maintaining a comparable reward–KL tradeoff. The resulting lesson is simple: budget should be concentrated on timesteps whose guidance can be made reliable, rather than on timesteps whose updates are later suppressed.

Validation Across Settings. In zeroth-order flow matching, the baseline bottleneck is uniform budget allocation across timesteps, even though the useful region of the trajectory depends on the reward. For GenEval [11], the reward is primarily semantic, so investing heavily in high-SNR timesteps is unnecessary; those steps are more tied to fine details than to the semantic structure the reward emphasizes. We therefore concentrate branching budget on the first few low-SNR timesteps, where semantic guidance is most useful. This redesign reaches GenEval =0.97=0.97 with a 5×5\times wall-clock speedup over TempFlow-GRPO (Fig. 15(a)).

In zeroth-order diffusion, the baseline bottleneck is the absence of branching: PCPO [20] uses a single sampled continuation at every reverse step, so each timestep receives a noisy point estimate of the reward signal. Ideally, one would branch at every reverse step, but doing so over the full trajectory (N=50N=50) is prohibitively expensive. We therefore introduce branching only at a sparse subset of steps and leave the rest unbranched, concentrating reward-bearing updates where they are most useful while keeping total compute manageable. This sparse-allocation design improves reward substantially faster while achieving a better reward–KL tradeoff (Fig. 15(b, c)).

In first-order methods, the baseline bottleneck is local Tweedie-based guidance, but this is partly obscured in the original evaluation settings, which are mostly aesthetic-heavy. Prior first-order methods [26, 27, 18] are evaluated either on purely aesthetic rewards or on HPSv2.1 [47] with prompt subsets such as hpd_photo_painting, where semantic demands are relatively weak. When we instead fine-tune on HPSv2.1 using GenEval training prompts, so that both aesthetic quality and semantic fidelity matter, performance drops sharply under original designs. In this setting, low-SNR timesteps can no longer be ignored: local Tweedie-based gradients become increasingly biased there, yet meaningful learning still has to occur at those steps. We therefore replace these local gradients with terminal-image reward gradients ∇𝒙0r​(𝒙0)\nabla_{{\bm{x}}_{0}}r({\bm{x}}_{0}), effectively moving to j=0j=0, which yields a practical reward score distillation update while reversing the inherited low-SNR downweighting1212 12 Although the exact quantity ∇𝒙tir​(𝒙0)\nabla_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}}r({\bm{x}}_{0}) would provide an unbiased first-order guidance signal, computing it requires a high-order Jacobian chain through the full denoising trajectory, which is both computationally expensive and potentially destabilizing, as noted in Poole et al. [31]. We therefore use the practical surrogate ∇𝒙0r​(𝒙0)\nabla_{{\bm{x}}_{0}}r({\bm{x}}_{0}); see Appendix E for details.. Across both flow-matching and diffusion backbones, this yields substantially faster reward improvement while remaining competitive in the reward–KL tradeoff (Fig. 5)1313 13 We display transition drift for first-order flow matching, since KL divergence is undefined for the VGG-Flow baseline [26]; see Appendices E.2 and F.1..

6 Discussion

Broadening the framework. RSM covers most affine flow-based RL fine-tuning methods, but several related objectives lie slightly outside its most direct formulation. Reward-weighted MLE methods such as ReFL [48] also fit within the broader Soft RL picture, although we did not study them here because they currently underperform the methods considered in this paper. Our method is also closely related to entropy-regularized optimal control in the absence of trust-region regularization (Appendix H.1), implying further unification with methods based on stochastic optimal control [7, 16, 43]. Related ideas may also extend beyond training-time alignment: Appendix H.2 shows that inference-time methods such as DNO [40] rely on closely related zeroth-order principles, but update the initial noise rather than the reverse-generation policy. DiffusionNFT is likewise closely related, as a form of reward-weighted regression connected to Soft RL; Appendix H.3 discusses this relation in more detail. Within first-order methods, another promising extension is to learn stronger value-gradient critics: existing auxiliary networks gϕg_{\phi} often collapse under weak supervision, and better bootstrapped or consistency-based targets may provide lower-variance guidance without the bias of shallow lookahead.

Better tuning of the design space. Our results show that the practical design space remains far from exhausted. In this paper, we did not perform exhaustive tuning or aggressive engineering; rather, we tested a small number of principled modifications, and even these already produced large gains. This suggests substantial headroom for more systematic tuning of RSM’s design space. Further simplification is also possible, for example by absorbing the trust-region term C2C_{2} into temporal weighting, as in GRPO-Guard [45] (see Eq. (107)). In addition, we optimized these choices under fixed samplers, even though sampler coefficients directly affect estimator variance and native timestep weights. Joint optimization of the sampler and training objective, as in PCPO (diffusion) [20], is therefore another promising direction.

Limitations. Although our redesign improves upon existing reward-based fine-tuning methods, it does not eliminate reward hacking. Our auxiliary evaluations suggest that the gains reported here are not driven by more aggressive reward hacking, but they do not establish emergent robustness to reward misspecification. More broadly, RSM does not unify all RL fine-tuning methods for flow-based models. It covers a broad class of score-matching-based approaches, but several important objectives remain outside its current scope, including offline preference-based methods such as Diffusion-DPO [44].

Broader Impact. Improving alignment of flow-based models enhances their ability to generate data with desired properties, hence better accommodating human needs throughout various application domains.

7 Conclusion

We introduced Reward Score Matching (RSM), a unified view of reward-based fine-tuning for flow and diffusion models. Under this view, many methods that are motivated from different perspectives reduce to the same underlying score-matching problem, with their main differences arising from how value guidance is estimated, weighted, and regularized across timesteps.

This perspective also clarifies the practical structure of the design space. In particular, it puts first-order and zeroth-order methods on common ground as different estimators of the same target, exposing shared bias–variance–compute tradeoffs that are otherwise obscured by method-specific derivations. It further shows that much of the remaining variation can be understood through three coupled design dimensions: estimator design, temporal weighting, and trust-region realization.

Guided by this framework, we identified several simplifications and principled redesigns that improve reward-based fine-tuning across representative differentiable-reward and black-box-reward settings, often with substantially better compute efficiency. Taken together, these results suggest that progress in this area depends less on introducing increasingly specialized objectives and more on understanding how to estimate, weight, and preserve reward-guided updates effectively. We aspire RSM to provide a common language for comparing existing methods, and a practical foundation for designing stronger ones.

Appendix B Main Proofs

B.1 Proof of Discretized affine flow SDE

Proof.

Consider a conditional affine flow 𝒙t:=ψt​(𝒙1|𝒙0)=at​𝒙0+bt​𝒙1{\bm{x}}_{t}:=\psi_{t}({\bm{x}}_{1}|{\bm{x}}_{0})=a_{t}{\bm{x}}_{0}+b_{t}{\bm{x}}_{1} with 𝒙1∼𝒩⁡(0,𝐈){\bm{x}}_{1}\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,{\mathbf{I}}). The corresponding flow ODE is described as

d​𝒙t=𝒗t​(𝒙t,t)​d​t\displaystyle d{\bm{x}}_{t}={\bm{v}}_{t}({\bm{x}}_{t},t)dt =a˙tat​𝒙t​d​t+(a˙t​bt2−at​b˙t​btat)​∇𝒙t​log⁡pt​(𝒙t)​d​t\displaystyle=\frac{\dot{a}_{t}}{a_{t}}{\bm{x}}_{t}dt+\left(\frac{\dot{a}_{t}b_{t}^{2}-a_{t}\dot{b}_{t}b_{t}}{a_{t}}\right)\nabla_{{\bm{x}}_{t}}\log p_{t}({\bm{x}}_{t})dt
=A⁡(t)​𝒙t​d​t+B⁡(t)​𝒔​(𝒙t,t).\displaystyle=A(t){\bm{x}}_{t}dt+B(t){\bm{s}}({\bm{x}}_{t},t). (31)

From Song et al. [37], the corresponding flow SDE that matches the same marginal density across time tt is

d​𝒙t\displaystyle d{\bm{x}}_{t} =[𝒗t​(𝒙t,t)−12​gt​𝒔​(𝒙t,t)]​d​t+gt​d​𝒘t\displaystyle=[{\bm{v}}_{t}({\bm{x}}_{t},t)-\frac{1}{2}g_{t}{\bm{s}}({\bm{x}}_{t},t)]dt+\sqrt{g_{t}}d{\bm{w}}_{t} (32)
=[A⁡(t)​𝒙t+(B⁡(t)−12​gt)​𝒔​(𝒙t,t)]​d​t+gt​d​𝒘t\displaystyle=[A(t){\bm{x}}_{t}+(B(t)-\frac{1}{2}g_{t}){\bm{s}}({\bm{x}}_{t},t)]dt+\sqrt{g_{t}}d{\bm{w}}_{t} (33)
=[A⁡(t)​𝒙t+B~​(t)​𝒔​(𝒙t,t)]​d​t+gt​d​𝒘t.\displaystyle=[A(t){\bm{x}}_{t}+\tilde{B}(t){\bm{s}}({\bm{x}}_{t},t)]dt+\sqrt{g_{t}}d{\bm{w}}_{t}. (34)

where we set B~​(t)=B⁡(t)−0.5​gt\tilde{B}(t)=B(t)-0.5g_{t}. Note that B~​(t)=B​(t)\tilde{B}(t)=B(t) when gt=0g_{t}=0 (i.e. ODE).

Consider an integrating factor Φ⁡(t)=exp⁡(∫A⁡(τ)​𝑑τ)\Phi(t)=\exp{(\int A(\tau)d\tau)}. For 𝒚t=Φ​(t)−1​𝒙t{\bm{y}}_{t}=\Phi(t)^{-1}{\bm{x}}_{t}, we apply Ito derivative and obtain

d​𝒚t\displaystyle d{\bm{y}}_{t} =Φ​(t)−1​d​𝒙t+𝒙t​d​Φ​(t)−1\displaystyle=\Phi(t)^{-1}d{\bm{x}}_{t}+{\bm{x}}_{t}d\Phi(t)^{-1} (35)
=Φ​(t)−1​[A⁡(t)​𝒙t​d​t+B~​(t)​𝒔​(𝒙t,t)​d​t+gt​d​𝒘t]−A⁡(t)​Φ​(t)−1​𝒙t​d​t\displaystyle=\Phi(t)^{-1}[A(t){\bm{x}}_{t}dt+\tilde{B}(t){\bm{s}}({\bm{x}}_{t},t)dt+\sqrt{g_{t}}d{\bm{w}}_{t}]-A(t)\Phi(t)^{-1}{\bm{x}}_{t}dt (36)
=Φ​(t)−1​[B~​(t)​𝒔​(𝒙t,t)​d​t+gt​d​𝒘t],\displaystyle=\Phi(t)^{-1}[\tilde{B}(t){\bm{s}}({\bm{x}}_{t},t)dt+\sqrt{g_{t}}d{\bm{w}}_{t}], (37)

where the first equality holds as d​Φ​(t)−1​d​𝒙t≈0d\Phi(t)^{-1}d{\bm{x}}_{t}\approx 0. Thus, by integrating both sides from ss to tt, we have

𝒙t\displaystyle{\bm{x}}_{t} =Φ⁡(t)Φ⁡(s)​𝒙s+Φ⁡(t)Φ⁡(s)​∫stΦ⁡(s)Φ⁡(r)​B~​(r)​𝒔​(𝒙r,r)​𝑑r+Φ⁡(t)Φ⁡(s)​∫stΦ⁡(s)Φ⁡(r)​gr​d​𝒘r\displaystyle=\frac{\Phi(t)}{\Phi(s)}{\bm{x}}_{s}+\frac{\Phi(t)}{\Phi(s)}\int_{s}^{t}\frac{\Phi(s)}{\Phi(r)}\tilde{B}(r){\bm{s}}({\bm{x}}_{r},r)dr+\frac{\Phi(t)}{\Phi(s)}\int_{s}^{t}\frac{\Phi(s)}{\Phi(r)}\sqrt{g_{r}}d{\bm{w}}_{r} (38)
≈Φ⁡(t)Φ⁡(s)​𝒙s+[Φ⁡(t)Φ⁡(s)​∫stΦ⁡(s)Φ⁡(r)​B~​(r)​𝑑r]​𝒔​(𝒙s,s)+Φ⁡(t)Φ⁡(s)​∫stΦ⁡(s)Φ⁡(r)​gr​d​𝒘r,\displaystyle\approx\frac{\Phi(t)}{\Phi(s)}{\bm{x}}_{s}+\left[\frac{\Phi(t)}{\Phi(s)}\int_{s}^{t}\frac{\Phi(s)}{\Phi(r)}\tilde{B}(r)dr\right]{\bm{s}}({\bm{x}}_{s},s)+\frac{\Phi(t)}{\Phi(s)}\int_{s}^{t}\frac{\Phi(s)}{\Phi(r)}\sqrt{g_{r}}d{\bm{w}}_{r}, (39)

where we assume 𝒔⁡(𝒙r,r)≈𝒔⁡(𝒙s,s){\bm{s}}({\bm{x}}_{r},r)\approx{\bm{s}}({\bm{x}}_{s},s) which corresponds to the first-order exponential integrator underlying DPM-solver. Note that higher-order DPM-solvers use higher-order approximations here.

For conditional flow models, A⁡(t)=a˙t/atA(t)=\dot{a}_{t}/a_{t} and Φ⁡(t)=at\Phi(t)=a_{t} by definition. Thus, the discretized SDE simplifies to:

𝒙t=atas​𝒙s+[atas​∫stasar​B~​(r)​𝑑r]​𝒔​(𝒙s,s)+at​∫st1ar​gr​d​𝒘r,\displaystyle{\bm{x}}_{t}=\frac{a_{t}}{a_{s}}{\bm{x}}_{s}+\left[\frac{a_{t}}{a_{s}}\int_{s}^{t}\frac{a_{s}}{a_{r}}\tilde{B}(r)dr\right]{\bm{s}}({\bm{x}}_{s},s)+a_{t}\int_{s}^{t}\frac{1}{a_{r}}\sqrt{g_{r}}d{\bm{w}}_{r}, (40)

where the first term denotes a scaled previous sample, the second term denotes a score function, and the third term denotes the Gaussian noise with zero mean and covariance σs2​𝐈\sigma_{s}^{2}{\mathbf{I}} where σs2=at2​∫stgrar2​𝑑r\sigma_{s}^{2}=a_{t}^{2}\int_{s}^{t}\frac{g_{r}}{a^{2}_{r}}dr. Hence, by setting s=tis=t_{i} and t=ti−1t=t_{i-1}, we can express the general form of transition density p⁡(𝒙ti−1|𝒙ti)p({\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}}|{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}) as

p(𝒙ti−1|𝒙ti)=𝒩(κ⁡(ti)​𝒙ti+Ω⁡(ti)​𝒔​(𝒙ti)⏟=:𝝁ti​(𝒙ti),σti2𝐈).\displaystyle p({\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}}|{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}})={\mathcal{N}}(\underbrace{\kappa(t_{i}){\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}+\Omega(t_{i}){\bm{s}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i}})}_{=:\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t_{i}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i}})},\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}{\mathbf{I}}). (41)

B.2 Proof of Proposition 3.1

We first need the following lemma for the zero-mean score identity.

Lemma B.1 (Zero-mean score identity under tail regularity).

Fix 𝐱∈ℝd{\bm{x}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and let p(⋅∣𝐱)p(\cdot\mid{\bm{x}}) be a conditional density on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} (with respect to Lebesgue measure) such that:

  1. 1.

    ∫ℝdp⁡(𝒖∣𝒙)​𝑑𝒖=1\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}p({\bm{u}}\mid{\bm{x}})\,d{\bm{u}}=1;

  2. 2.

    p(⋅∣𝒙)p(\cdot\mid{\bm{x}}) is differentiable in 𝒖{\bm{u}}, and ∫ℝd|∂ujp⁡(𝒖∣x)|​𝑑𝒖<∞​ for ​∀j∈{1,…,d}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\big|\partial_{u_{j}}p({\bm{u}}\mid x)\big|\,d{\bm{u}}<\infty\ \text{ for }\ \forall j\in\{1,\dots,d\};

  3. 3.

    For ∀j\forall j, for almost every 𝒖−j∈ℝd−1{\bm{u}}_{-j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d-1}, lim𝒖j→±∞p⁡(uj,𝒖−j∣𝒙)=0\lim_{{\bm{u}}_{j}\to\pm\infty}p(u_{j},{\bm{u}}_{-j}\mid{\bm{x}})=0.

Then the conditional score has zero mean:

𝔼𝒖∼p(⋅∣𝒙)[∇𝒖logp(𝒖∣𝒙)]=𝟎.\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{u}}\sim p(\cdot\mid{\bm{x}})}\big[\nabla_{\bm{u}}\log p({\bm{u}}\mid{\bm{x}})\big]=\mathbf{0}. (42)
Proof.

For each jj,

𝔼p(⋅∣𝒙)[∂ujlogp(𝒖∣𝒙)]=∫ℝdp(𝒖∣𝒙)∂ujp⁡(𝒖∣𝒙)p⁡(𝒖∣𝒙)d𝒖=∫ℝd∂ujp(𝒖∣𝒙)d𝒖,\mathbb{E}_{p(\cdot\mid{\bm{x}})}[\partial_{u_{j}}\log p({\bm{u}}\mid{\bm{x}})]=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}p({\bm{u}}\mid{\bm{x}})\,\frac{\partial_{u_{j}}p({\bm{u}}\mid{\bm{x}})}{p({\bm{u}}\mid{\bm{x}})}\,d{\bm{u}}=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\partial_{u_{j}}p({\bm{u}}\mid{\bm{x}})\,d{\bm{u}},

where the equality is valid wherever p⁡(𝒖∣𝒙)>0p({\bm{u}}\mid{\bm{x}})>0, and condition 2 justifies the integral. Write 𝒖=(uj,𝒖−j){\bm{u}}=(u_{j},{\bm{u}}_{-j}) and apply Fubini:

∫ℝd∂ujp⁡(𝒖∣𝒙)​𝑑𝒖=∫ℝd−1(∫ℝ∂ujp⁡(uj,𝒖−j∣x)​d​uj)​d​𝒖−j.\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\partial_{u_{j}}p({\bm{u}}\mid{\bm{x}})\,d{\bm{u}}=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d-1}}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}}\partial_{u_{j}}p(u_{j},{\bm{u}}_{-j}\mid x)\,du_{j}\right)d{\bm{u}}_{-j}.

For fixed 𝒖−j{\bm{u}}_{-j}, the inner integral is a 1D integral of a derivative, hence by the fundamental theorem of calculus,

∫ℝ∂ujp⁡(uj,𝒖−j∣x)​d​uj=[p⁡(uj,𝒖−j∣x)]uj=−∞uj=+∞.\int_{\mathbb{R}}\partial_{u_{j}}p(u_{j},{\bm{u}}_{-j}\mid x)\,du_{j}=\Big[p(u_{j},{\bm{u}}_{-j}\mid x)\Big]_{u_{j}=-\infty}^{u_{j}=+\infty}.

By condition 3, this boundary term is 00 for almost every 𝒖−j{\bm{u}}_{-j}, so the outer integral is 00. Since this holds for each jj, we conclude Eq. (42). ∎

Proposition 3.6 formalizes the ideal case underlying residual-corrected first-order methods: if gϕg_{\phi} exactly captures the Jensen-gap residual induced by Tweedie’s formula, then both current-state and one-step first-order guidance are unbiased. In practice, however, Appendix G.1 shows that the learned residual term is negligible, so this consistency condition is not realized empirically.

Thus, for existing methods, the Jensen gap

Vt​(𝒙t)−r⁡(𝒙^0​(𝒙t))\displaystyle V_{t}({\bm{x}}_{t})-r(\hat{\bm{x}}_{0}({\bm{x}}_{t})) =α​log⁡(∫exp⁡(r⁡(𝒙0)α)​pref​(𝒙0∣𝒙t)​d​𝒙0)−α​log⁡(exp⁡(r​(𝒙^0​(𝒙t))α))\displaystyle=\alpha\log\Big(\int\exp\Big(\frac{r({\bm{x}}_{0})}{\alpha}\Big)p^{\text{ref}}({\bm{x}}_{0}\mid{\bm{x}}_{t})d{\bm{x}}_{0}\Big)-\alpha\log\Big(\exp\Big(\frac{r(\hat{\bm{x}}_{0}({\bm{x}}_{t}))}{\alpha}\Big)\Big) (52)

is not meaningfully closed.

Under exact residual correction, Eq. (21) recovers the intended ℒforward\mathcal{L}_{\text{forward}} of Residual ∇\nabla-DB. Choosing gϕ​(⋅)=𝟎g_{\phi}(\cdot)=\mathbf{0} yields SQDF. γt=1,gϕ​(⋅)=𝟎\gamma_{t}=1,g_{\phi}(\cdot)=\mathbf{0} returns to the case where we approximate the value function with only Tweedie’s formula, as in DPS [6].

B.4 Proof of Theorem 3.7

We prove that the REINFORCE-based estimator is an unbiased estimator of the gradient of the soft value function. This aligns with the practical reality that existing implementations of Soft PPO and GRPO [9, 24] treat the KL penalty as additive intermediate rewards rather than solving the exact log-sum-exp Soft Bellman equation.

B.5 Convergence of Policy Iteration

Section 3 and Appendix B characterize the reward-guided target and its associated optimal guidance as fixed-point identities of the optimum p⋆p^{\star}. In practice, however, RL-based fine-tuning methods sample from the current policy pθp^{\theta} and update that policy using the RSM loss. We therefore rely on prior policy optimization theory for convergence guarantees. TRPO [36] was originally derived from a monotonic improvement perspective, and subsequent theory established that exact TRPO converges to the optimal policy in entropy-regularized MDPs [29]. More recent results established global convergence guarantees for PPO-clip and its variants under neural function approximation [17]. Accordingly, our core theory specifies the fixed point that the reward score matching update is designed to target, while convergence of the resulting iterative optimization procedure is justified by prior works rather than proven in this paper.

𝚿ti{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathbf{\Psi}_{t_{i}}} and C2​(ti)C_{2}(t_{i}) appear singular due to 1/α1/\alpha, but these quantities appear only through products C1​(ti)​𝚿tiC_{1}(t_{i}){\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathbf{\Psi}_{t_{i}}} and C1​(ti)​C2​(ti)C_{1}(t_{i})C_{2}(t_{i}) in Eq. (15). Therefore, when α=0\alpha=0, the canonical gradient remains the correct object for interpreting optimization dynamics, although the literal decomposition from Eq. (11) no longer strictly applies.

C.1 First-order Methods

C.1.1 Residual ∇\nabla-DB

The relationship between Residual ∇\nabla-DB and Soft RL has bene briefly discussed in Appendix D of Liu et al. [27]. We rewrite the objective by mapping forward and backward GFlowNet processes (PF,PB)(P_{F},P_{B}) to reverse sampling and forward noising, respectively.

Residual ∇\nabla-DB minimizes a weighted sum of four terms:
ℒtotal​(θ,ϕ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{total}}(\theta,\phi) =wF​ℒforward​(θ,ϕ)+wB​ℒbackward​(θ,ϕ)+ℒterminal​(ϕ)+wR​ℒreg​(θ),\displaystyle=w_{F}\mathcal{L}_{\text{forward}}(\theta,\phi)+w_{B}\mathcal{L}_{\text{backward}}(\theta,\phi)+\mathcal{L}_{\text{terminal}}(\phi)+w_{R}\mathcal{L}_{\text{reg}}(\theta), (63)
ℒforward​(θ,ϕ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{forward}}(\theta,\phi) =𝔼ti,𝒙ti,ϵti​[‖∇𝒙ti−1ℓtiθ​(𝒙ti−1,𝒙ti)−𝒢GFN_F​(𝒙ti,ϵti)‖2],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{t_{i},{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}},{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}}}\Big[\Big\|\nabla_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}}}\ell_{t_{i}}^{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}},{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}})-\mathcal{G}_{\text{GFN\_F}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i}},{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}})\Big\|^{2}\Big], (64)
ℒbackward​(θ,ϕ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{backward}}(\theta,\phi) =𝔼ti,𝒙ti,ϵti​[‖∇𝒙tiℓtiθ​(𝒙ti−1,𝒙ti)+𝒢GFN_B​(𝒙ti)‖2],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{t_{i},{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}},{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}}}\Big[\Big\|\nabla_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}}\ell_{t_{i}}^{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}},{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}})+\mathcal{G}_{\text{GFN\_B}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i}})\Big\|^{2}\Big], (65)
ℒterminal​(ϕ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{terminal}}(\phi) =𝔼𝒙0​[‖gϕ​(𝒙0)‖2],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{x}}_{0}}[\|g_{\phi}({\bm{x}}_{0})\|^{2}], (66)
ℒreg​(θ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{reg}}(\theta) =𝔼ti,𝒙ti​[‖ϵtiθ−ϵtiθ†‖2]=𝔼ti,𝒙ti​[(1−α¯ti)​‖𝒔tiθ−𝒔tiθ†‖2],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{t_{i},{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}}[\|{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}}^{\theta}-{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}}^{\theta^{\dagger}}\|^{2}]=\mathbb{E}_{t_{i},{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}}[(1-\bar{\alpha}_{t_{i}})\|{\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\theta}-{\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\theta^{\dagger}}\|^{2}], (67)
where ℓ\ell, gradient fields 𝒢\mathcal{G} and Gaussian reparameterization are:
ℓtiθ​(𝒙ti−1,𝒙ti)\displaystyle\ell_{t_{i}}^{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}},{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}) :=log⁡pθ​(𝒙ti−1∣𝒙ti)−log⁡pref​(𝒙ti−1∣𝒙ti),\displaystyle:=\log p^{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}}\mid{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}})-\log p^{\mathrm{ref}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}}\mid{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}), (68)

𝒢GFN_B​(𝒙ti)\displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{\text{GFN\_B}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}) =1α​γ~ti​sg⁡(∇𝒙tir​(𝒙^0|ti))+gϕ​(𝒙ti),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\alpha}\tilde{\gamma}_{t_{i}}\operatorname{sg}(\nabla_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}}r(\hat{\bm{x}}_{0|t_{i}}))+g_{\phi}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}), (70)
𝒙ti−1\displaystyle{\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}} =𝝁tiθ+σti​ϵti,ϵti∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈).\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t_{i}}^{\theta}+\sigma_{t_{i}}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}},\quad{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}).

Pruning ℒbackward\mathcal{L}_{\text{backward}} and ℒterminal\mathcal{L}_{\text{terminal}}. ℒbackward\mathcal{L}_{\text{backward}} requires the gradient ∇𝒙tiℓtiθ​(𝒙ti−1,𝒙ti)\nabla_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}}\ell_{t_{i}}^{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}},{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}). Under the Gaussian reparameterization, 𝒙ti−1{\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}} depends on 𝒙ti{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}} through the model output, which introduces Jacobian terms of the form ∂ϵtiθ/∂𝒙ti\partial{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}}^{\theta}/\partial{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}} into ∇𝒙tiℓtiθ\nabla_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}}\ell_{t_{i}}^{\theta}. Consequently, ∇θℒbackward\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{backward}} involves higher-order derivatives, including mixed θ\theta-𝒙{\bm{x}} terms, rendering optimization numerically unstable and empirically ineffective. This is consistent with our ablation results: removing ℒbackward\mathcal{L}_{\text{backward}} does not degrade performance, whereas removing ℒforward\mathcal{L}_{\text{forward}} causes training to fail (Appendix G.1).

ℒterminal\mathcal{L}_{\text{terminal}} (Eq. (66)) is not parameterized by θ\theta and therefore contributes no gradient to the canonical loss term in Theorem 3.2. Moreover, as discussed in Appendix G.1, the outputs of gϕg_{\phi} are negligible in magnitude and do not affect the training dynamics.

Reduction to Reward Score Matching. ∇𝒙ti−1ℓtiθ\nabla_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}}}\ell_{t_{i}}^{\theta} can be expressed as a scaled score difference:

∇𝒙ti−1ℓtiθ​(𝒙ti−1,𝒙ti)=1σti2​(𝝁tiθ−𝝁tiref)=Ω⁡(ti)σti2​(𝒔tiθ−𝒔tiref).\nabla_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}}}\ell_{t_{i}}^{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}},{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}})=\frac{1}{\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t_{i}}^{\theta}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t_{i}}^{\text{ref}})=\frac{\Omega(t_{i})}{\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}}({\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\theta}-{\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\text{ref}}). (71)
∴ℒforward​(θ,ϕ)=𝔼ti,𝒙ti,ϵti​[Ω​(ti)2σti4​‖𝒔tiθ−(𝒔tiref+σti2Ω⁡(ti)​𝒢GFN_F​(𝒙ti,ϵti))‖2].\therefore\mathcal{L}_{\text{forward}}(\theta,\phi)=\mathbb{E}_{t_{i},{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}},{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}}}\Bigg[\frac{\Omega(t_{i})^{2}}{\sigma_{t_{i}}^{4}}\bigg\|{\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\theta}-\big({\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\text{ref}}+\frac{\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}}{\Omega(t_{i})}\,\mathcal{G}_{\text{GFN\_F}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i}},{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}})\big)\bigg\|^{2}\Bigg]. (72)

Thus, wF​ℒforward+wR​ℒregw_{F}\mathcal{L}_{\text{forward}}+w_{R}\mathcal{L}_{\text{reg}} is a special case of the canonical loss, with

𝚿ti=γ~ti​σti2α​Ω​(ti)​sg⁡(∇𝒙ti−1r​(𝒙^0|ti−1)),C1​(ti)=1d​Ω​(ti)2σti4,C2​(ti)=(1−α¯ti)​σti4Ω​(ti)2​wRwF,{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathbf{\Psi}_{t_{i}}}=\tilde{\gamma}_{t_{i}}\frac{\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}}{\alpha\Omega(t_{i})}\operatorname{sg}(\nabla_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}}}r(\hat{\bm{x}}_{0|t_{i-1}})),\quad C_{1}(t_{i})=\frac{1}{d}\frac{\Omega(t_{i})^{2}}{\sigma_{t_{i}}^{4}},\quad C_{2}(t_{i})=\frac{(1-\bar{\alpha}_{t_{i}})\sigma_{t_{i}}^{4}}{\Omega(t_{i})^{2}}\frac{w_{R}}{w_{F}}, (73)

where the factor 1d\frac{1}{d} arises implicitly from a torch.mean() operation over tensor dimensions.

C.1.2 SQDF

SQDF is motivated by the following objective, given in Eq. 11 of Kang et al. [18]:

ℒ(θ)=𝔼ti,𝒙ti,ϵti[−r(𝒙^0|ti−1)+α𝒟KL(pθ(𝒙ti−1∣𝒙ti)∥pref(𝒙ti−1∣𝒙ti))].\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{t_{i},{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}},{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}}}\big[-r(\hat{\bm{x}}_{0|t_{i-1}})+\alpha\mathcal{D}_{\text{KL}}(p^{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}}\mid{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}})\|p^{\text{ref}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}}\mid{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}))\big]. (74)

In the actual implementation, however, the transition mean 𝝁ti−1θ\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t_{i-1}}^{\theta} is reparameterized, and a stopgrad operation is applied to the Tweedie estimate inside the reward term. In addition, an attenuation factor γ~ti=γ~SQDFN​ti\tilde{\gamma}_{t_{i}}=\tilde{\gamma}_{\text{SQDF}}^{Nt_{i}} is introduced in the reward term for temporal credit assignment. To analyze the resulting optimization dynamics, we adopt the parameterization in Lemma 3.1.

ℒ(θ)=𝔼ti,𝒙ti,ϵti[−γ~tisg(∇𝒙ti−1r(𝒙^0|ti−1))⋅𝝁tiθ+α2​σti2∥𝝁ti−1θ−𝝁ti−1ref∥2].\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{t_{i},{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}},{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}}}\Big[-\tilde{\gamma}_{t_{i}}\ \operatorname{sg}(\nabla_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}}}r(\hat{\bm{x}}_{0|t_{i-1}}))\cdot\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t_{i}}^{\theta}+\frac{\alpha}{2\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}}\big\|\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t_{i-1}}^{\theta}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t_{i-1}}^{\text{ref}}\big\|^{2}\Big]. (75)

Substituting 𝝁ti−1θ−𝝁ti−1ref=Ω⁡(ti)​(𝒔tiθ−𝒔tiref)\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t_{i-1}}^{\theta}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t_{i-1}}^{\text{ref}}=\Omega(t_{i})({\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\theta}-{\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\text{ref}}) yields

𝔼[−γ~tisg(∇𝒙ti−1r(𝒙^0|ti−1))⋅(κ(ti)𝒙ti+Ω(ti)𝒔tiθ)+α​Ω​(ti)22​σti2∥𝒔tiθ−𝒔tiref∥2],\mathbb{E}\bigg[-\tilde{\gamma}_{t_{i}}\ \operatorname{sg}(\nabla_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}}}r(\hat{\bm{x}}_{0|t_{i-1}}))\cdot\big(\kappa(t_{i}){\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}+\Omega(t_{i}){\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\theta}\big)+\frac{\alpha\Omega(t_{i})^{2}}{2\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}}\big\|{\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\theta}-{\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\text{ref}}\big\|^{2}\bigg], (76)

Up to additive terms that do not contribute to the gradient, this is equivalent to:

𝔼ti,𝒙ti,ϵti​[α​Ω​(ti)22​σti2​‖𝒔tiθ−(𝒔tiref+γ~ti​σti2α​Ω​(ti)​sg⁡(∇𝒙ti−1r​(𝒙^0|ti−1)))‖2].\mathbb{E}_{t_{i},{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}},{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}}}\left[\frac{\alpha\Omega(t_{i})^{2}}{2\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}}\left\|{\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\theta}-\left({\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\text{ref}}+\tilde{\gamma}_{t_{i}}\frac{\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}}{\alpha\Omega(t_{i})}\ \operatorname{sg}(\nabla_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}}}r(\hat{\bm{x}}_{0|t_{i-1}}))\right)\right\|^{2}\right]. (77)

Therefore, SQDF is a special case of the canonical loss, with

𝚿ti=γ~ti​σti2α​Ω​(ti)​sg⁡(∇𝒙ti−1r​(𝒙^0|ti−1)),C1​(ti)=α2​Ω​(ti)2σti2,C2​(ti)=0.{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathbf{\Psi}_{t_{i}}}=\tilde{\gamma}_{t_{i}}\frac{\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}}{\alpha\Omega(t_{i})}\ \operatorname{sg}(\nabla_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}}}r(\hat{\bm{x}}_{0|t_{i-1}})),\quad C_{1}(t_{i})=\frac{\alpha}{2}\frac{\Omega(t_{i})^{2}}{\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}},\quad C_{2}(t_{i})=0. To facilitate comparison, we rewrite the VGG-Flow objectives using the parameterization Gϕ​(𝒙ti)≜−γ~ti​sg​(∇𝒙tir​(𝒙^0|ti))−gϕ​(𝒙ti)G^{\phi}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i}})\triangleq-\tilde{\gamma}_{t_{i}}\ \text{sg}\big(\nabla_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}}r(\hat{\bm{x}}_{0|t_{i}})\big)-g^{\phi}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}).

ℒconsistency​(ϕ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{consistency}}(\phi) =𝔼ti,𝒙ti​‖∂∂t​Gϕ​(𝒙t)|t=ti+[∇Gϕ​(𝒙ti)]⊤​(𝒗tiref+1λ​Gϕ​(𝒙ti))+[∇𝒙ti𝒗tiref]⊤​Gϕ​(𝒙ti)‖2,\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{t_{i},{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}}\Big\|\frac{\partial}{\partial t}G^{\phi}({\bm{x}}_{t})\Big|_{t=t_{i}}+[\nabla G^{\phi}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i}})]^{\top}({\bm{v}}_{t_{i}}^{\text{ref}}{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}+}\frac{1}{\lambda}G^{\phi}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}))+[\nabla_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}}{\bm{v}}_{t_{i}}^{\text{ref}}]^{\top}G^{\phi}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i}})\Big\|^{2}, (79)

C.2 Zeroth-order Methods

We now turn to policy-gradient-based methods. As the canonical zeroth-order base case, we begin with a KL-regularized REINFORCE objective, which is the natural policy-gradient analogue of the Soft RL formulation under our unified transition parameterization. Note that this is a strictly on-policy algorithm. This yields the fundamental zeroth-order effective value guidance, after which all variants can be understood as straightforward modifications within the design space of RSM.

C.2.1 KL-regularized REINFORCE

We formulate REINFORCE [39, 46] in the KL-regularized form used by Algorithm 1 (Soft PPO) of Uehara et al. [41]. Using our general parameterization, the objective is

ℒ(θ)=𝔼𝒙ti∼pθ,ϵti:1[−r(𝒙0)+α∑i=1N𝒟KL(pθ(𝒙ti−1|𝒙ti)∥pref(𝒙ti−1|𝒙ti))].\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}\sim p^{\theta},{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i:1}}}\left[-r({\bm{x}}_{0})+\alpha\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathcal{D}_{\text{KL}}(p^{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}}|{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}})\|p^{\text{ref}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}}|{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}))\right]. (84)

For Gaussian transitions with fixed covariance σti2​𝐈\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}\mathbf{I}, each KL term reduces to

α2​‖1σti​(𝝁ti−1θ​(𝒙ti)−𝝁ti−1ref​(𝒙ti))‖2.\frac{\alpha}{2}\|\frac{1}{\sigma_{t_{i}}}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t_{i-1}}^{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i}})-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t_{i-1}}^{\text{ref}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}))\|^{2}. (85)

The REINFORCE gradient of the reward term is

∇θ𝔼𝒙ti∼pθ,ϵti:1[−r(𝒙0)]=𝔼𝒙ti∼pθ,ϵti:1[−r(𝒙0)∇θlogpθ(𝒙ti−1|𝒙ti)].\nabla_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}\sim p^{\theta},{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i:1}}}[-r({\bm{x}}_{0})]=\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}\sim p^{\theta},{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i:1}}}\left[-r({\bm{x}}_{0})\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}}|{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}})\right]. (86)

Since

∇θ​log​pθ​(𝒙ti−1|𝒙ti)=(𝒙ti−1−𝝁ti−1θ)⊤​1σti2​∇θ𝝁ti−1θ=(1σti​ϵti)⊤​∇θ𝝁ti−1θ,\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}}|{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}})=({\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t_{i-1}}^{\theta})^{\top}\frac{1}{\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}}\nabla_{\theta}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t_{i-1}}^{\theta}=(\frac{1}{\sigma_{t_{i}}}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}})^{\top}\nabla_{\theta}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t_{i-1}}^{\theta}, (87)

combining the reward and KL terms yields

∇θℒ​(θ)=𝔼τ​[(−r⁡(𝒙0)​1σti​ϵti+α​1σti2​(𝝁ti−1θ−𝝁ti−1ref))⊤​∇θ𝝁ti−1θ],\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\tau}\left[\Big(-r({\bm{x}}_{0})\frac{1}{\sigma_{t_{i}}}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}}+\alpha\frac{1}{\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t_{i-1}}^{\theta}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t_{i-1}}^{\text{ref}})\Big)^{\top}\nabla_{\theta}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t_{i-1}}^{\theta}\right], (88)

where τ={𝒙ti}i=0N\tau=\{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}\}_{i=0}^{N} denotes the trajectory induced by θ\theta.

Substituting the unified parameterization 𝝁ti−1θ=κ⁡(ti)​𝒙ti+Ω⁡(ti)​𝒔tiθ\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t_{i-1}}^{\theta}=\kappa(t_{i}){\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}+\Omega(t_{i}){\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\theta} from Lemma 3.1, we obtain

∇θℒ​(θ)\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}(\theta) =𝔼τ​[(−r⁡(𝒙0)​1σti​ϵti+α​Ω​(ti)σti2​(𝒔tiθ−𝒔tiref))⊤​Ω​(ti)​∇θ𝒔tiθ]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\tau}\left[\Big(-r({\bm{x}}_{0})\frac{1}{\sigma_{t_{i}}}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}}+\frac{\alpha\Omega(t_{i})}{\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}}({\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\theta}-{\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\text{ref}})\Big)^{\top}\Omega(t_{i})\nabla_{\theta}{\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\theta}\right] (89)
=𝔼τ​[α​Ω​(ti)2σti2​(𝒔tiθ−𝒔tiref−σtiα​Ω​(ti)​r​(𝒙0)​ϵti)⊤​∇θ𝒔tiθ].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\tau}\left[\frac{\alpha\Omega(t_{i})^{2}}{\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}}\Big({\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\theta}-{\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\text{ref}}-\frac{\sigma_{t_{i}}}{\alpha\Omega(t_{i})}r({\bm{x}}_{0}){\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}}\Big)^{\top}\nabla_{\theta}{\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\theta}\right]. (90)

This is precisely the gradient of the weighted squared loss

ℒ⁡(θ)=𝔼τ​[α​Ω​(ti)22​σti2​‖(𝒔tiθ−(𝒔tiref+𝚿ti))‖2],\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\tau}\left[\frac{\alpha\Omega(t_{i})^{2}}{2\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}}\|({\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\theta}-({\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\text{ref}}+{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathbf{\Psi}_{t_{i}}}))\|^{2}\right], (91)

with

𝚿ti=σtiα​Ω​(ti)​r​(𝒙0)​ϵti,C1​(ti)=α2​Ω​(ti)2σti2,C2​(ti)=0.{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathbf{\Psi}_{t_{i}}}=\frac{\sigma_{t_{i}}}{\alpha\Omega(t_{i})}r({\bm{x}}_{0}){\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}},\quad C_{1}(t_{i})=\frac{\alpha}{2}\frac{\Omega(t_{i})^{2}}{\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}},\quad C_{2}(t_{i})=0. (92)

In relation to Lemma 3.1, REINFORCE corresponds to the zeroth-order estimation of the lookahead value gradient,

𝔼𝒙ti−1∼p𝒙ti⋆​[∇𝒙ti−1𝑽ti−1⋆​(𝒙ti−1)]=𝔼⁡[r⁡(𝒙0)​ϵti]σti,\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}}\sim p^{\star}_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}}}\left[\nabla_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}}}\boldsymbol{V}^{\star}_{t_{i-1}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}})\right]=\frac{\mathbb{E}[r({\bm{x}}_{0}){\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}}]}{\sigma_{t_{i}}}, (93)

using a point estimation for the expectation.

C.2.2 Clipped log-ratio surrogate

We next consider the clipped log-ratio surrogate used by PCPO-base [20]. Denoting the old-policy ratio by

ρti=pθ​(𝒙ti−1∣𝒙ti)pθ†​(𝒙ti−1∣𝒙ti),\rho_{t_{i}}=\frac{p_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}}\mid{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}})}{p_{\theta^{\dagger}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}}\mid{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}})}, (94)

the clipped objective is

ℒclip-log​(θ)={𝔼𝒙ti∼pθ†,ϵti​[−r⁡(𝒙0)​log⁡ρti+α​Ω​(ti)22​σti2​‖𝒔tiθ−𝒔tiref‖2]if ​(−ξ≤log⁡ρti≤ξ)or ​(log⁡ρti<−ξ∧r⁡(𝒙0)≥0)or ​(log⁡ρti>ξ∧r⁡(𝒙0)≤0),𝔼𝒙ti∼pθ†,ϵti​[α​Ω​(ti)22​σti2​‖𝒔tiθ−𝒔tiref‖2]otherwise.\mathcal{L}_{\text{clip-log}}(\theta)=\begin{cases}\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}\sim p^{\theta^{\dagger}},\,{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}}}\!\left[-r({\bm{x}}_{0})\log\rho_{t_{i}}+\dfrac{\alpha\Omega(t_{i})^{2}}{2\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}}\left\|{\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\theta}-{\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\mathrm{ref}}\right\|^{2}\right]&\begin{aligned} &\text{if }\big(-\xi\leq\log\rho_{t_{i}}\leq\xi\big)\\ &\quad\text{or }\big(\log\rho_{t_{i}}<-\xi\land r({\bm{x}}_{0})\geq 0\big)\\ &\quad\text{or }\big(\log\rho_{t_{i}}>\xi\land r({\bm{x}}_{0})\leq 0\big),\end{aligned}\\[4.30554pt] \mathbb{E}_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}\sim p^{\theta^{\dagger}},\,{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}}}\!\left[\dfrac{\alpha\Omega(t_{i})^{2}}{2\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}}\left\|{\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\theta}-{\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\mathrm{ref}}\right\|^{2}\right]&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} (95)

where

C.2.3 Variants

EPG. EPG [4] is a variant of REINFORCE, which extends it to the loose on-policy setting, and uses a control variate for variance reduction. Its loss can be written as

ℒEPG​(θ)=𝔼τ∼pθ†​[sg⁡(ρti)​α​Ω​(ti)22​σ​(ti)2​‖𝒔tiθ−(𝒔tiref+𝚿ti)‖2],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{EPG}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim p^{\theta^{\dagger}}}\Big[\operatorname{sg}(\rho_{t_{i}})\,\frac{\alpha\Omega(t_{i})^{2}}{2\sigma(t_{i})^{2}}\big\|{\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\theta}-\big({\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\mathrm{ref}}+{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathbf{\Psi}_{t_{i}}}\big)\big\|^{2}\Big], (100)

with the same 𝚿ti\mathbf{\Psi}_{t_{i}} as KL-regularized REINFORCE. Compared to REINFORCE, the only modification is the multiplicative stop-gradient importance ratio, which does not produce gradients itself.

PPO, GRPO. Huang et al. [17] proved that the KL-regularized PPO loss

𝔼𝒙ti∼pθ†,ϵti​[max⁡(−ρti​r​(𝒙0),−clipξ​(ρti)​r​(𝒙0))+α​Ω​(ti)22​σti2​‖𝒔tiθ−𝒔tiref‖2]\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}\sim p^{\theta^{\dagger}},{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}}}[\max\big(-\rho_{t_{i}}r({\bm{x}}_{0}),-\text{clip}_{\xi}(\rho_{t_{i}})r({\bm{x}}_{0})\big)+\frac{\alpha\Omega(t_{i})^{2}}{2\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}}\left\|{\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\theta}-{\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\text{ref}}\right\|^{2}] (101)

is equivalent to

ℒclip​(θ)={𝔼𝒙ti∼pθ†,ϵti​[−r⁡(𝒙0)​(ρti−1)+α​Ω​(ti)22​σti2​‖𝒔tiθ−𝒔tiref‖2]if ​(1−ξ≤ρti≤1+ξ)or ​(ρti<1−ξ∧r⁡(𝒙0)≥0)or ​(ρti>1+ξ∧r⁡(𝒙0)≤0),𝔼𝒙ti∼pθ†,ϵti​[α​Ω​(ti)22​σti2​‖𝒔tiθ−𝒔tiref‖2]otherwise.\mathcal{L}_{\text{clip}}(\theta)=\begin{cases}\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}\sim p^{\theta^{\dagger}},\,{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}}}\!\left[-r({\bm{x}}_{0})(\rho_{t_{i}}-1)+\dfrac{\alpha\Omega(t_{i})^{2}}{2\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}}\left\|{\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\theta}-{\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\mathrm{ref}}\right\|^{2}\right]&\begin{aligned} &\text{if }\big(1-\xi\leq\rho_{t_{i}}\leq 1+\xi\big)\\ &\quad\text{or }\big(\rho_{t_{i}}<1-\xi\land r({\bm{x}}_{0})\geq 0\big)\\ &\quad\text{or }\big(\rho_{t_{i}}>1+\xi\land r({\bm{x}}_{0})\leq 0\big),\end{aligned}\\[4.30554pt] \mathbb{E}_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}\sim p^{\theta^{\dagger}},\,{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}}}\!\left[\dfrac{\alpha\Omega(t_{i})^{2}}{2\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}}\left\|{\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\theta}-{\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\mathrm{ref}}\right\|^{2}\right]&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} (102)

up to constants independent of θ\theta. Therefore, PPO simply replaces the log-ratio term in Eq. (95) with ρti−1\rho_{t_{i}}-1. For Gaussian transitions,

ρti−1=exp⁡(−Ω⁡(ti)σti​(𝒔tiθ−𝒔tiθ†)⊤​ϵti−Ω​(ti)22​σti2​‖𝒔tiθ−𝒔tiθ†‖2)−1.\rho_{t_{i}}-1=\exp\left(-\frac{\Omega(t_{i})}{\sigma_{t_{i}}}({\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\theta}-{\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\theta^{\dagger}})^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}}-\frac{\Omega(t_{i})^{2}}{2\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}}\left\|{\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\theta}-{\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\theta^{\dagger}}\right\|^{2}\right)-1. (103)

Directly optimizing this exponential is numerically unstable. In practice, diffusion/flow-based PPO and GRPO implementations [3, 9, 50, 24] use an extremely tight clipping threshold (e.g., ξ=10−4\xi=10^{-4}). Under such tight clipping, the first-order approximation exp⁡(x)−1≈x\exp(x)-1\approx x incurs error of order ξ2/2\xi^{2}/2 for the interior regime 1−ξ≤ρti≤1+ξ1-\xi\leq\rho_{t_{i}}\leq 1+\xi, as well as for clipped cases where the loss is already fixed at the clipping boundary1717 17 The remaining non-clipped sign-consistent regimes, (ρti<1−ξ∧r⁡(𝒙0)≥0CLOSE(\rho_{t_{i}}<1-\xi\land r({\bm{x}}_{0})\geq 0) and (ρti>1+ξ∧r⁡(𝒙0)≤0)(\rho_{t_{i}}>1+\xi\land r({\bm{x}}_{0})\leq 0), admit a looser bound. Empirically, however, Lee and Ye [20] observe that |ρti−1|<0.01|\rho_{t_{i}}-1|<0.01 throughout training due to a low learning rate, so the approximation error remains small in practice.. Under this necessary approximation, PPO / GRPO reduce to the clipped log-ratio surrogate in Eq. (98), and therefore have the same unified terms as Eq. (99).

PCPO-reweight. For flow-matching models, PCPO explicitly reweights the policy loss by

γti=wnew​(ti)w⁡(ti),wnew​(ti)=ζ​Δ​ti,ζ=∑i=1Nw⁡(ti).\gamma_{t_{i}}=\frac{w_{\text{new}}(t_{i})}{w(t_{i})},\qquad w_{\text{new}}(t_{i})=\zeta\Delta t_{i},\qquad\zeta=\sum_{i=1}^{N}w(t_{i}). (104)

See Appendix D.3 for more details. This modifies only the effective guidance and anchor strength:

𝚿ti=γti​σtiα​Ω​(ti)​r​(𝒙0)​ϵti,C1​(ti)=α2​Ω​(ti)2σti2,C2​(ti)=γti​r⁡(𝒙0)α.{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathbf{\Psi}_{t_{i}}}=\gamma_{t_{i}}\frac{\sigma_{t_{i}}}{\alpha\Omega(t_{i})}r({\bm{x}}_{0}){\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}},\quad C_{1}(t_{i})=\frac{\alpha}{2}\frac{\Omega(t_{i})^{2}}{\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}},\quad C_{2}(t_{i})=\gamma_{t_{i}}\frac{r({\bm{x}}_{0})}{\alpha}. (105)

For diffusion models, PCPO implicitly reweights h⁡(ti)h(t_{i}) by modifying the variance schedule σti\sigma_{t_{i}} to σti′\sigma^{\prime}_{t_{i}}. Its effect is summarized in Table 1.

GRPO-Guard. GRPO-Guard observes that log⁡ρti\log\rho_{t_{i}} is negatively biased by the KL term between the current and old policies, which empirically shifts its mean below zero. To correct this, it centers and rescales the log-ratio as

σti​(log⁡ρti−𝔼⁡[log⁡ρti]),\sigma_{t_{i}}\big(\log\rho_{t_{i}}-\mathbb{E}[\log\rho_{t_{i}}]\big),

and additionally reweights the policy term by 1/Δ​ti1/\Delta t_{i}. Under the clipped log-ratio objective, this yields

ℒ⁡(θ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\theta) ={𝔼⁡[α​Ω​(ti)22​σti2​‖𝒔tiθ−(𝒔tiref+𝚿ti)‖2]if −ξ≤σti​(log⁡ρti−𝔼⁡[log⁡ρti])≤ξ,𝔼⁡[α​Ω​(ti)22​σti2​‖𝒔tiθ−𝒔tiref‖2]otherwise,\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\alpha\Omega(t_{i})^{2}}{2\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}}\left\|{\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\theta}-\big({\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\text{ref}}+{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathbf{\Psi}_{t_{i}}}\big)\right\|^{2}\right]&\text{if }-\xi\leq\sigma_{t_{i}}\big(\log\rho_{t_{i}}-\mathbb{E}[\log\rho_{t_{i}}]\big)\leq\xi,\\[6.0pt] \mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\alpha\Omega(t_{i})^{2}}{2\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}}\left\|{\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\theta}-{\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\text{ref}}\right\|^{2}\right]&\text{otherwise},\end{cases} (106)

with

𝚿ti=γti​σtiα​Ω​(ti)​r​(𝒙0)​ϵti,C1​(ti)=α2​Ω​(ti)2σti2,C2​(ti)=0,{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathbf{\Psi}_{t_{i}}}=\gamma_{t_{i}}\frac{\sigma_{t_{i}}}{\alpha\Omega(t_{i})}r({\bm{x}}_{0}){\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}},\quad C_{1}(t_{i})=\frac{\alpha}{2}\frac{\Omega(t_{i})^{2}}{\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}},\quad C_{2}(t_{i})=0, (107)

where γti=σti​Ω​(ti)Δ​ti\gamma_{t_{i}}=\frac{\sigma_{t_{i}}\Omega(t_{i})}{\Delta t_{i}}. Thus, GRPO-Guard explicitly removes the old-policy anchor term.

TempFlow-GRPO. TempFlow-GRPO introduces trajectory branching: starting from a deterministic ODE trajectory, it revisits each intermediate latent 𝒙ti{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}, injects one-step SDE noise to generate multiple descendants, and then deterministically denoises each descendant to the terminal state for reward evaluation1818 18 Although TempFlow-GRPO presents the sampling order differently, it is functionally equivalent to this interpretation.. This is precisely a multi-particle lookahead estimator in our framework. Note that TempFlow-GRPO does not explicitly average value-guidance vectors; instead, it applies an L2L_{2} regression loss to multiple reward-weighted point estimates. However, because the gradient of a sum of squared errors is centered at the sample mean, this optimization is functionally equivalent to regressing toward the average of those particle-wise targets. Hence, under RSM, TempFlow-GRPO implicitly realizes a zeroth-order lookahead value-guidance estimator with branching width Ki>1K_{i}>1, together with heuristic temporal reweighting γ⁡(ti)=94​σti\gamma(t_{i})=\frac{9}{4}\sigma_{t_{i}}. This yields

𝚿ti=γti​σtiα​Ω​(ti)​(1Ki​∑k=1Kir⁡(𝒙0(k))​ϵti(k)),C1​(ti)=α2​Ω​(ti)2σti2,C2​(ti)=γti​r⁡(𝒙0)α.{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathbf{\Psi}_{t_{i}}}=\gamma_{t_{i}}\frac{\sigma_{t_{i}}}{\alpha\Omega(t_{i})}\Big(\frac{1}{K_{i}}\sum_{k=1}^{K_{i}}r({\bm{x}}_{0}^{(k)}){\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}}^{(k)}\Big),\quad C_{1}(t_{i})=\frac{\alpha}{2}\frac{\Omega(t_{i})^{2}}{\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}},\quad C_{2}(t_{i})=\gamma_{t_{i}}\frac{r({\bm{x}}_{0})}{\alpha}. (108)

BranchGRPO. BranchGRPO likewise uses multiple descendants to estimate a zeroth-order lookahead guidance term, but differs from TempFlow-GRPO in that its branching is recursive rather than one-step from each revisited parent latent. Under the same RSM view, it therefore realizes a multi-particle estimator form:

𝚿ti=σtiα​Ω​(ti)​(1Ki​∑k=1Kir⁡(𝒙0(k))​ϵti(k)),C1​(ti)=α2​Ω​(ti)2σti2,C2​(ti)=r⁡(𝒙0)α.{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathbf{\Psi}_{t_{i}}}=\frac{\sigma_{t_{i}}}{\alpha\Omega(t_{i})}\Big(\frac{1}{K_{i}}\sum_{k=1}^{K_{i}}r({\bm{x}}_{0}^{(k)}){\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}}^{(k)}\Big),\quad C_{1}(t_{i})=\frac{\alpha}{2}\frac{\Omega(t_{i})^{2}}{\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}},\quad C_{2}(t_{i})=\frac{r({\bm{x}}_{0})}{\alpha}. (109)

C.3 Remark on parameters.

To address the discrepancies in naming conventions across Soft RL and GFlowNet literature, we have unified the notation for components that serve identical functions. Table 3 maps the various notations found in prior works to the single, unified notation used in this text.

Entropy Regularization (α\alpha): While often denoted as β\beta (inverse temperature) or 1/β1/\beta in Soft RL contexts, we adopt α\alpha to strictly control the degree of entropy regularization1919 19 SQDF [18] apply mean reduction over the latent dimension dd for only entropy regularization, and omit the 12\frac{1}{2} coefficient for the KL divergence. Consequently, their reported α\alpha corresponds to an effective regularization weight of 2​α/d2\alpha/d. .

Downweighting Factor (γ~t\tilde{\gamma}_{t}): We rename VGG-Flow’s one-step reward estimation factor from ηt\eta_{t} to γ~t\tilde{\gamma}_{t} to align with the conventions established by Residual ∇\nabla-DB and SQDF.

Reward Value (r⁡(⋅)r(\cdot)): In diffusion fine-tuning GFlowNet literature, the reward is often interpreted as the log of the GFlowNet reward. We use r⁡(⋅)r(\cdot) directly to refer to this value.

Appendix D Parameterizations

D.1 Ω\Omega Derivations for Popular Samplers

In this section, we provide step-by-step derivations of the scaling factor Ω⁡(ti)\Omega(t_{i}) for two widely used sampling algorithms: DDIM applied to VP-SDE (e.g., Stable Diffusion 1.5) and Euler Discrete applied to Rectified Flow (e.g., Stable Diffusion 3).

From Proposition 3.1, the relationship between the optimal score 𝒔ti⋆{\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\star}, the reference score 𝒔tiref{\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\text{ref}}, and the value gradient is established via the conditional transition mean 𝝁ti−1\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t_{i-1}}. When 𝝁ti−1\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t_{i-1}} can be expressed in the form 𝝁ti−1=κ⁡(ti)​𝒙ti+Ω⁡(ti)​𝒔ti\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t_{i-1}}=\kappa(t_{i}){\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}+{\Omega(t_{i})}{\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}, the guidance term simplifies to:

𝒔ti⋆=𝒔tiref+σti2α​Ω​(ti)​∇𝒙ti−1Vti−1​(𝒙ti−1).{\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\star}={\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\text{ref}}+\frac{\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}}{\alpha\Omega(t_{i})}\nabla_{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}}}V_{t_{i-1}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}}). (110)

The specific value of Ω⁡(ti)\Omega(t_{i}) depends on the choice of noise schedule and numerical solver.

D.1.1 DDIM Sampler (VP-SDE)

For the DDIM sampler applied to a VP-SDE, the transition from 𝒙ti{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}} to 𝒙ti−1{\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}} is defined as:

𝒙ti−1=α¯ti−1​𝒙^0​(𝒙ti)+1−α¯ti−1−σti2​ϵtiθ+σti​ϵti{\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}}=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t_{i-1}}}\hat{{\bm{x}}}_{0}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i}})+\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t_{i-1}}-\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}}^{\theta}+\sigma_{t_{i}}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}} (111)

where 𝒙^0​(𝒙ti)=𝒙ti−1−α¯ti​ϵtiθα¯ti\hat{{\bm{x}}}_{0}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i}})=\frac{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}-\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t_{i}}}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}}^{\theta}}{\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t_{i}}}} is the Tweedie estimate of the clean data, and ϵti∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈){\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}) is the injected noise.

We can rewrite the conditional transition mean 𝝁ti−1​(𝒙ti)\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t_{i-1}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}) as:

𝝁ti−1​(𝒙ti)\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t_{i-1}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}) =α¯ti−1​(𝒙ti−1−α¯ti​ϵtiθα¯ti)+1−α¯ti−1−σti2​ϵtiθ\displaystyle=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t_{i-1}}}\left(\frac{{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}-\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t_{i}}}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}}^{\theta}}{\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t_{i}}}}\right)+\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t_{i-1}}-\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}}^{\theta}
=α¯ti−1α¯ti​𝒙ti−(α¯ti−1α¯ti​1−α¯ti−1−α¯ti−1−σti2)​ϵtiθ\displaystyle=\sqrt{\frac{\bar{\alpha}_{t_{i-1}}}{\bar{\alpha}_{t_{i}}}}{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}-\left(\sqrt{\frac{\bar{\alpha}_{t_{i-1}}}{\bar{\alpha}_{t_{i}}}}\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t_{i}}}-\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t_{i-1}}-\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}}\right){\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t_{i}}^{\theta}
=α¯ti−1α¯ti​𝒙ti+(α¯ti−1α¯ti​1−α¯ti−1−α¯ti−1−σti2)​1−α¯ti⏟Ω⁡(ti)​𝒔tiθ.\displaystyle=\sqrt{\frac{\bar{\alpha}_{t_{i-1}}}{\bar{\alpha}_{t_{i}}}}{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}+\underbrace{\left(\sqrt{\frac{\bar{\alpha}_{t_{i-1}}}{\bar{\alpha}_{t_{i}}}}\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t_{i}}}-\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t_{i-1}}-\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}}\right)\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t_{i}}}}_{\Omega(t_{i})}{\bm{s}}_{t_{i}}^{\theta}. (112)

D.1.2 SDE-DPM-Solver++ (VP-SDE)

To further demonstrate the generality of our framework, we derive Ω⁡(ti)\Omega(t_{i}) for SDE-DPM-Solver++ [28], a higher-order solver supported by Residual ∇\nabla-DB.

Let at=α¯ta_{t}=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}} and bt2=1−at2b_{t}^{2}=1-a_{t}^{2} for the brevity. Let λt=log⁡(at/bt)\lambda_{t}=\log(a_{t}/b_{t}) be log-SNR and h=λti−1−λtih=\lambda_{t_{i-1}}-\lambda_{t_{i}}.
